slides.title: Complex housing reduces repetitive behavior
body: **Stereotypy** is repetitive behavior with little variation and no obvious immediate goal. Bailoo and colleagues recorded female C57 and SWISS mice in barren, nesting-only, enriched, or super-enriched housing. Video scoring expressed stereotypy as a proportion of active time, separating repetition from simple inactivity.

The super-enriched condition connected two cages and provided shelters, climbing opportunities, tunnels, and regularly changed objects. Stereotypy was greatly reduced in both strains compared with the other conditions; nesting material or modest enrichment did not produce a consistent equivalent reduction.

Bar mouthing, circling, twirling and back-flipping were scored separately. Their expression differed between strains, while the largest reduction in total stereotypy occurred with the most extensive resources. Enclosure structure changed which actions mice could perform and how their active time was distributed among those actions.

slides.title: Mice actively use opportunities in complex cages
body: **Environmental enrichment** supplies resources that allow more species-typical activity than basic food, water, and bedding alone. In the same experiment, mice were scored as engaged when they contacted an enrichment item or manipulated the housing environment, including bedding in barren cages.

Mice in the super-enriched condition engaged with their environment during more than 85% of observed intervals on average. Barren-housed mice engaged least, while nesting and enriched cages supported intermediate levels. The comparison therefore measures use of resources rather than their mere presence.

The engagement category included being inside, on or under a shelter as well as manipulating objects. Complex housing supplied protected resting locations and opportunities to climb and explore. These resources supported different activities within the same cage, explaining why engagement encompassed more than locomotion alone.

slides.title: Hormone responses depend on mouse strain
body: **Glucocorticoids** are adrenal hormones involved in the physiological response to stress; corticosterone is a major rodent glucocorticoid. Bailoo and colleagues measured its fecal metabolites, products formed after hormone processing, to compare endocrine outcomes without taking blood during the measurement.

SWISS mice in barren and nesting-only cages had higher metabolite concentrations than mice in enriched and super-enriched cages. C57 mice did not exhibit the same consistent housing effect. Concentrations were reported in ng per 0.05 g of feces, and excretion reflects secretion delayed by approximately 8–10 hours.

Cage changing reorganizes the animals’ immediate surroundings, and hormone secretion reaches the feces after a physiological delay. Collection timing therefore connects the endocrine measurement to this husbandry event. The strain comparison separates a shared reduction in stereotypy from a hormone response that depended on genetic background.

slides.title: Different welfare measures can disagree
body: **Perseveration** is inappropriate persistence in a response pattern when changing responses would be useful. Mice completed a two-choice guessing task in which reward probabilities depended on their preceding choices. This assessed inhibitory control separately from home-cage stereotypy.

Housing condition and stereotypy level did not consistently predict the perseveration score. A separate spatial judgment task trained mice to approach a rewarded location and withhold approach at a nonrewarded location, then tested three intermediate locations. Enrichment did not cause a consistent shift toward approaching ambiguous cues across both strains.

A **judgment task** measures responses to cues between previously rewarded and unrewarded locations. Inhibitory control in the guessing task and approach to ambiguous locations tested different processes from repetitive movement. Housing altered home-cage behavior while these decision measures remained comparatively unchanged, separating behavioral flexibility from the amount of visible repetition.

slides.title: Full social contact predicts less macaque stereotypy
body: Full-contact pair housing was associated with less stereotypy than either solitary housing or protected contact. The protected-contact partition had bars 4.5 cm apart but did not provide the same association with reduced stereotypy. Foraging devices were also associated with a lower likelihood of stereotypy when present.

Gottlieb and colleagues assessed captive rhesus macaques using 5-minute behavioral observations over 11 years. **Motor stereotypies** were repeated whole-body movements such as pacing, rocking, and somersaulting. Housing categories distinguished solitary cages, protected contact through bars, and full access to a social partner.

All housing categories allowed visual access to another macaque. Full-contact pairing additionally permitted direct interaction, whereas the partition restricted the range of available social actions. Foraging devices supplied another opportunity to obtain resources through activity. Social access and food-directed activity each accompanied lower stereotypy in the observed population.

slides.title: Temperament predicts stereotypy expression
body: **Behavioral inhibition** describes withdrawal from unfamiliar situations. After observing stereotypy, investigators presented a novel food item and recorded inspection for 3 minutes. Macaques inspecting within 5 seconds were classified as bold; later inspection was moderate, and no inspection was inhibited.

Bold and moderate responders were more likely to express motor stereotypy than inhibited responders. The association remained in a model that also included housing, enrichment, rearing history, ancestry, and age. A visibly active monkey and a withdrawn monkey can therefore express an adverse environment differently.

Inspection included deliberate visual, olfactory or tactile examination of the novel food. Eating was not required. The classification therefore concerned willingness to investigate an unfamiliar item, distinguishing novelty-directed activity from consumption. That response profile accompanied differences in how repetitive movement was expressed in the home cage.

slides.title: Early rearing predicts later repetitive behavior
body: Nursery-reared and indoor mother-reared monkeys had the highest modeled risk of motor stereotypy, whereas corral-reared animals had the lowest. Current housing and foraging conditions were included alongside early history, so the analysis did not attribute every adult difference to the cage occupied at observation.

The macaque analysis also classified the environment experienced during the first 6 months of life. Outdoor corral rearing provided a large social group, while other categories included sheltered groups, indoor groups, nursery rearing, and indoor mother rearing. These histories differed before the adult observations began.

Early rearing supplied different combinations of space, social partners and contact with mothers or caregivers. Those experiences preceded the adult housing observations by years. Adult stereotypy consequently reflected a developmental history as well as current social and foraging opportunities, linking present behavior to resources experienced at different life stages.

slides.title: Captivity changes hormone responses in wild birds
body: Baseline corticosterone rose after 2 weeks relative to capture. Restraint-induced concentrations depended on both time in captivity and life-history stage, including moult, winter, and breeding. Birds also lost body mass during captivity, while recorded behaviors changed over the same period.

Lattin and colleagues followed wild house sparrows during 4 weeks of laboratory captivity. **Baseline corticosterone** was sampled within 3 minutes of capture or room entry; the acute stress response was sampled after 30 minutes of standardized restraint. These measurements distinguish resting hormone levels from a response to challenge.

The endocrine response changed over weeks while feeding, body mass and maintenance behavior were tracked over the same interval. Baseline secretion and the response to restraint describe different operating conditions of the stress system. Their contrasting associations with feeding connect physiological regulation to coping with a sustained environmental transition.

slides.title: PET measures dopamine binding in sparrow striatum
body: **Dopamine** is a transmitter that modifies neural signaling through several receptor classes. The **striatum** is a forebrain region involved in behavior and action selection. Investigators used positron emission tomography, or PET, to localize a radioactive ligand that binds dopamine D2 receptors in living sparrows.

The ligand, carbon-11 raclopride, accumulated more strongly in striatum than in the cerebellar reference region. Giving haloperidol at 0.5 mg/kg displaced striatal binding during a scan, supporting the interpretation that the signal included receptor-specific binding rather than only nonspecific tracer distribution.

**Binding potential** estimates specific ligand binding relative to a region with little specific binding. Endogenous dopamine and the injected ligand compete for available receptor sites. Regional accumulation and displacement by haloperidol together identified a dopamine-receptor signal, connecting the anatomical location of the striatum with a measurable neurochemical response.

slides.title: Dopamine binding changes with captivity and season
body: Larger declines in binding were associated with more feather ruffling and beak wiping during captivity. Higher initial binding predicted more feeding at early assessments but lower body mass later, so receptor binding did not track every behavioral and physiological endpoint in the same direction.

Sparrows underwent a first D2-receptor PET scan 24 hours after capture, with a subset scanned again after 4 weeks. Striatal binding potential decreased in moulting birds, while comparable decreases were not detected in winter or breeding birds. The neural response to captivity therefore differed by life-history stage.

Moult, winter and breeding impose different biological demands on the same species. The selective decline during moult links captivity-associated receptor binding to life-history state. Its associations with feeding and maintenance behavior further connect the striatal measurement with particular actions, while body mass provides a separate physiological outcome.

slides.title: Repeated restraint increases neuronal firing gain
body: Current pulses lasted 800 milliseconds. Firing gain increased from 0.68 to 1.55 action potentials per 100 pA in repeatedly stressed rats. A single restraint session did not produce the same increase. **Action potentials** are brief regenerative electrical signals, so greater gain means more neural output for comparable injected current.

Rosenkranz and colleagues restrained male rats for 20 minutes on 7 days within a 9-day period; controls received comparable handling without restraint. Intracellular recordings then measured **excitability**, the number of action potentials elicited by a controlled input, in principal neurons of the lateral amygdala.

The increased spike output remained when neurons were held at −70 mV. Matching this starting voltage isolated responsiveness to the current pulse from a shift in resting potential. Repeated restraint therefore changed the transformation of depolarizing input into action potentials, increasing the gain of amygdala neuronal output.

slides.title: Resting membrane changes do not explain all stress effects
body: **Input resistance** describes how strongly a neuron’s membrane voltage changes for a small injected current. Repeatedly stressed rats had increased input resistance in lateral-amygdala neurons, and the membrane time constant was longer, indicating a changed response to subthreshold inputs that do not trigger spikes.

However, matching voltage and examining these passive properties did not account for the full increase in spike output. Blocking fast inhibitory inputs through GABA-A-related chloride conductances also left a stress-related excitability difference. **GABA-A receptors** are transmitter-gated channels that contribute to rapid inhibitory signaling in this preparation.

Input resistance governs the size of a subthreshold voltage response, while the membrane time constant governs its duration. Spike generation additionally depends on active conductances recruited during firing. The persistent difference after the tested inhibitory blockade directed the explanation toward intrinsic regulation of action-potential output.

slides.title: Stress weakens the brake after a burst of spikes
body: An **afterhyperpolarization** is a period of more negative membrane voltage after spiking that restrains further firing. Calcium entering during activity can activate potassium channels; outward potassium current then contributes to this brake. The medium and slow afterhyperpolarizations were reduced after repeated restraint.

The slow component averaged 2.6 mV in controls and 0.7 mV in stressed rats. Pharmacologically blocking calcium entry reduced the afterhyperpolarization and diminished the excitability difference between groups. These interventions support a calcium-dependent contribution to the stress-related increase in firing.

The fast voltage recovery after a single spike remained comparatively unchanged, while the medium and slow brakes following a burst were weakened. A smaller post-burst potassium-dependent brake permits additional spikes during sustained input. The stress effect therefore concerned the temporal regulation of repeated firing rather than every phase of the action potential.

slides.title: Enhancing the spike brake reverses hyperexcitability
body: The investigators administered **1-EBIO**, a compound that enhances calcium-activated potassium-channel activity, after recording baseline excitability. At 10 mg/kg it increased the medium afterhyperpolarization and reduced excessive spike output in stressed rats toward the control range. Vehicle-treated animals provided a comparison for injection effects.

The same systemic treatment also altered elevated-plus-maze behavior. Repeatedly stressed vehicle-treated rats spent about 10 seconds in open arms, whereas treated stressed rats spent about 65 seconds. Total arm entries did not show a corresponding group difference, limiting a simple explanation based on general movement.

The parallel increase in open-arm exploration occurred without a corresponding increase in total arm entries. Channel modulation thus altered both sustained neuronal responsiveness and the distribution of exploratory behavior under the tested stress conditions.

slides.title: Early stress and enrichment alter dendritic spines
body: **Dendrites** receive neuronal inputs, and **dendritic spines** are small protrusions that commonly host excitatory synapses. Golgi staining visualized principal neurons in the basolateral amygdala. Investigators counted spines along 60 µm segments of primary and secondary dendrites in adulthood.

Early maternal separation increased spine density under both standard and enriched rearing conditions. Enrichment shifted density downward overall but did not abolish the separation-associated increase. The structural outcome therefore differed from a simple description in which enrichment completely erased every stress effect.

Primary dendrites emerge from the cell body, and secondary dendrites branch from them. Counting spines per micrometre measures the density of potential input sites along each sampled segment. Early separation and enrichment shifted this local structure in opposing directions, producing an adult anatomical pattern that retained both developmental influences.

slides.title: Receptor localization changes without a protein increase
body: A **glucocorticoid receptor**, or GR, is an intracellular receptor whose nuclear localization can influence gene regulation. Investigators immunolabeled GR and identified nuclei with a DNA stain in adult basolateral-amygdala sections. They measured the fraction of nuclei containing detectable GR signal.

Early separation reduced the fraction with nuclear GR, while enrichment had an opposing effect. Total GR protein measured in tissue extracts did not differ clearly across the same treatment comparisons. Receptor location within cells can therefore change without a corresponding detectable increase in overall protein abundance.

The DNA stain identified nuclei, and receptor labeling identified GR signal within those nuclei. Tissue extracts instead combined protein across cellular compartments. Separation and enrichment changed the nuclear fraction while total protein remained similar, linking early experience to where the receptor was located within adult amygdala cells.

slides.title: Enrichment changes a plasticity-related protein signal
body: **Brain-derived neurotrophic factor**, or BDNF, is a signaling protein associated with neuronal growth and synaptic plasticity. slides.title: A day of isolation changes excitatory synapses
body: Matthews and colleagues isolated mice from cage mates for 24 hours, then recorded identified dopamine neurons in the **dorsal raphe nucleus**, a midbrain region. They measured glutamate-evoked currents through AMPA and NMDA receptors, two receptor classes that support excitatory synaptic signaling.

The AMPA-to-NMDA current ratio increased in dorsal-raphe dopamine neurons after isolation, including when isolation occurred in the familiar home cage. A comparable change was not detected in the sampled ventral-tegmental dopamine neurons. A novel cage without isolation did not reproduce the same increase.

**Rectification** is an asymmetric dependence of current flow on membrane voltage. The authors’ hypothesis was that isolation increased AMPA receptors lacking the GluR2 subunit, which permits calcium entry. Preferential suppression by NASPM and altered rectification supported that receptor contribution, linking social conditions to the properties of excitatory synapses.

slides.title: Raphe dopamine neurons signal to forebrain targets
body: **Optogenetics** uses a light-sensitive protein to control selected neurons. Channelrhodopsin-2, a light-gated cation channel, was expressed in dorsal-raphe dopamine neurons. Blue-light pulses depolarized the cells and evoked action potentials, connecting a defined intervention to neuronal output.

Labeled axons reached the **bed nucleus of the stria terminalis** and the **central amygdala**, forebrain regions involved in behavioral state and threat-related processing. Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, an electrochemical measurement, detected dopamine release in these targets during stimulation with 5-millisecond light pulses.

Axonal labeling identified the target regions, and stimulation-induced dopamine release confirmed that the projections carried a transmitter output. Light-gated cation entry first depolarized the manipulated neurons, and brief pulses then recruited their axons. This sequence connected cellular activation with neurochemical signaling in the forebrain targets.

slides.title: Dopamine neurons can also release glutamate
body: Dorsal-raphe dopamine neurons were not limited to dopamine transmission. Optical stimulation of their axon terminals evoked rapid **excitatory postsynaptic currents**, electrical currents in target cells driven by excitatory synaptic input. Recordings were made in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis and central amygdala.

A 5-millisecond light pulse evoked short-latency currents recorded at −70 mV. The currents persisted with tetrodotoxin and 4-aminopyridine, a combination used to test direct terminal-mediated transmission, and were consistent with glutamate release. Slower inhibitory responses reflected additional local circuit recruitment.

**Co-transmission** means a defined neuronal population communicates through more than one transmitter. Tetrodotoxin blocked sodium-dependent spikes, while potassium-channel blockade allowed illuminated terminals to release transmitter directly. The surviving excitatory currents identified a fast glutamatergic connection alongside the dopamine output of this raphe population.

slides.title: Lower fish density does not guarantee better welfare
body: Sen Sarma and colleagues reared zebrafish at 1, 3, or 6 fish/L with barren, gravel, plant, or gravel-plus-plant conditions. **Stocking density** is the number of fish per unit of water volume. Fish reared at 1 fish/L were longer and heavier than those at the higher densities. This growth result might appear favorable when considered alone. However, the same low-density groups also expressed more aggression and stronger cortisol release during a group challenge.

The growth and social outcomes diverged within the same housing comparison. More length and mass at 1 fish/L accompanied more attacks and stronger group-challenge cortisol release. Density changed a network of biological outcomes, connecting nutritional growth with the social interactions occurring around those growing fish.

slides.title: Confinement prolongs aggression after crayfish defeat
body: Bacqué-Cazenave and colleagues paired previously isolated, size-matched male crayfish in a confined arena for 20 minutes. Encounters progressed from exploration to fighting, then to continued attacks after one animal retreated. **Social defeat** refers here to the outcome of this observed contest rather than an inferred subjective report.

After defeat, the loser largely stopped fighting while the winner continued approaches and attacks. The loser responded with escapes. The prolonged post-defeat phase differed from mutual fighting, because one animal repeatedly attempted to withdraw while remaining within its opponent’s reach.

After withdrawal, the loser’s behavior shifted toward escape while the winner continued pursuit. The 33 × 23 × 20 cm arena kept the animals within repeated contact. Confinement therefore sustained an asymmetric interaction after the initial contest had ended, linking available separation distance to the sequence of attacks and escapes.

slides.title: Defeated crayfish avoid illuminated spaces
body: Losers spent about 18% of their time in illuminated arms, compared with about 30% for winners and 32% for isolated controls. The drug chlordiazepoxide increased light-arm exploration in defeated animals, with saline injections controlling for the administration procedure.

After pairing, crayfish explored a plus maze containing dark and illuminated arms. **Anxiety-like behavior** was operationalized as stronger light avoidance and more retreats at dark–light boundaries. Winners and previously isolated animals provided comparisons for the defeated animals.

The defensive response persisted into a separate maze after the contest. Dark–light boundaries elicited retreats, and reduced occupation of illuminated arms supplied a second measure of avoidance. Pharmacological sensitivity connected this post-encounter pattern to a modifiable behavioral state rather than only to movements made during fighting.

slides.title: Post-defeat attacks predict later avoidance
body: More attacks during the post-defeat harassment phase were associated with less subsequent light-arm exploration. Duration of fighting did not show the same relationship. Thus, the measured consequence was more closely associated with what happened after withdrawal than with time spent in the initial contest.

The pairing observations allowed attacks before and after defeat to be separated. Investigators related the winner’s approaches and attacks to the loser’s later time in illuminated maze arms. This comparison tested whether sustained hostile contact, rather than fighting duration alone, tracked the defensive state.

Defeat separated two phases with different interaction patterns: reciprocal fighting and pursuit of an animal attempting to withdraw. Post-defeat attacks tracked later avoidance more closely than the duration of mutual fighting. Recording the sequence identifies continued exposure after retreat as a distinct biological event within the encounter.

slides.title: Serotonin contributes to the post-defeat state
body: **Serotonin**, also called 5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT, is a transmitter that modulates neural circuits. Brain serotonin was measured after the 20-minute pairing. Concentrations averaged about 236 pg/mg in isolated crayfish, 486 pg/mg in winners, and 691 pg/mg in losers.

Before pairing, methysergide, a broad serotonin-receptor antagonist, was given to the animal expected to lose. Compared with saline controls, treated defeated animals explored illuminated arms more and retreated less. They still lost the contest, separating the defensive state from the act of retreating during defeat.

A **receptor antagonist** reduces signaling through the receptors it targets. Methysergide altered later light avoidance despite preserving the loss of the contest. Serotonin-receptor signaling therefore contributed to the post-defeat defensive response, separating modulation of the later behavioral state from the contest outcome itself.

slides.title: A single serotonin cell modulates a motor network
body: In a separate crayfish study, researchers stimulated an identified serotonergic neuron in the first abdominal ganglion while recording walking-leg motor output. A **ganglion** is a cluster of neuronal cell bodies. Immunostaining and intracellular labeling confirmed that the recorded cell contained serotonin.

Current pulses drove the cell to fire initially at up to 40 Hz, then adapt toward about 17 Hz. Motor neurons in the connected postural network increased, decreased, or maintained their activity during this stimulation. Serotonin therefore did not impose a single uniform direction of motor response.

The retained coxo-basipodite chordotonal organ detected movement near the base of a walking leg. Stretching its sensory strand supplied position-related input to the central network. Stimulating an identified serotonergic cell while recording this network connected transmitter-neuron firing to the regulation of a specific postural response.

slides.title: Serotonin can amplify sensory-driven motor responses
body: A **motor neuron** carries neural output toward muscle, while an **excitatory postsynaptic potential** is a depolarizing response to synaptic input. In some depressor motor neurons, stimulation of the serotonergic cell depolarized the membrane and increased input resistance. The depressor network contributes to downward leg movement.

In the published example, membrane voltage changed from −83.2 to −75.6 mV, and the sensory-driven response increased from about 0.99 to 1.64 mV. Responses to movement of the retained proprioceptor were measured before and during serotonergic-cell stimulation in the same preparation.

Greater input resistance produces a larger voltage response to a given synaptic current. Depolarization also places the membrane closer to spike threshold, and slower decay prolongs the sensory input’s influence. These changes acted together in the excited cells, amplifying the pathway from proprioceptor activity to depressor motor output.

slides.title: The same serotonin input can suppress other neurons
body: Other depressor motor neurons responded to the same identified serotonin-cell stimulation with **hyperpolarization**, a shift to more negative voltage, and reduced input resistance. Sensory-driven responses became smaller rather than larger. These opposing effects occurred within the tested motor system.

In one recorded example, the reflex-related voltage response declined from about 0.077 to 0.045 mV. Synaptic potentials also decayed faster. Reduced voltage responsiveness and a more negative baseline can jointly decrease the influence of a sensory input on the cell’s motor output.

A more negative membrane voltage moves the cell farther from spike threshold, while lower resistance reduces the voltage response to input. Faster synaptic decay shortens its influence. The authors’ hypothesis links the opposing motor-neuron responses to differences in receptor location and local serotonin signaling within the same postural network.

slides.title: Bees learn different outcomes for odor mixtures
body: Bateson and colleagues trained honeybees to distinguish two mixtures of 1-hexanol and 2-octanone. One mixture predicted sucrose; the other predicted a less favorable outcome such as quinine. **Proboscis extension**, extending the feeding mouthparts, served as the measured response rather than locomotor approach.

The rewarded and negative cues used opposite 1:9 and 9:1 mixtures, with three intermediate mixtures presented without reinforcement during testing. These ambiguous odors tested generalization between learned outcomes. After training, experimental bees were shaken for 60 seconds while controls remained undisturbed.

Training assigned different outcomes to mixtures of the same two odorants before disturbance occurred. The intermediate mixtures then tested how the learned classification extended between those outcomes. Shaking changed the animal’s state after acquisition, allowing the test to measure altered responses to previously learned and ambiguous sensory cues.

slides.title: Acute disturbance biases responses to ambiguous odors
body: A **judgment bias** is a change in how an animal responds to an uncertain cue associated with possible favorable or unfavorable outcomes. Following 60 seconds of shaking, bees were tested within 5 minutes using the trained odors and three intermediate mixtures.

Shaken bees were less likely to extend the proboscis to the negative cue and the intermediate odor nearest it. Responses to the rewarded cue were not detectably reduced. The selective pattern limits an explanation based only on a general inability or unwillingness to extend the feeding mouthparts.

The effect was strongest near the negative end of the trained odor continuum, while the rewarded cue retained its response. A general failure to extend the proboscis would have affected that positive response as well. The authors’ hypothesis is that acute disturbance shifted the bees’ expectations toward unfavorable outcomes under ambiguity.

slides.title: Bee monoamine changes are not circuit measurements
body: In a separate group of bees, researchers measured **hemolymph**, the circulating fluid of insects, after the same shaking treatment. Dopamine, octopamine, serotonin, and tyramine were assayed. **Octopamine** is a signaling molecule with important roles in insect modulation and reward-related learning.

Around 300 seconds after shaking, dopamine, octopamine, and serotonin concentrations were reduced, whereas tyramine did not show the same clear reduction. The sampling time matched the period when the behavioral tests were performed. These physiological changes accompanied the treatment that altered judgment.

The treatment changed several modulators together, connecting a brief disturbance with a physiological state extending beyond the immediate shaking event.

slides.title: Octopuses learn places associated with injury
body: Crook tested _Octopus bocki_ in chambers with distinct visual patterns. **Conditioned place avoidance** measures whether an animal later avoids a location associated with an adverse event. Initial preferences were assessed before conditioning, allowing later choices to be compared with each animal’s earlier behavior.

A 0.5% acetic-acid injection in an arm was paired with the initially preferred chamber; saline injection provided a procedural control. On a later free-choice test, acid-treated octopuses reduced their time in the previously preferred chamber compared with controls.

Assigning the acid-associated event to the initially preferred chamber tested whether adverse experience could reverse an existing location preference. The later reduction in occupancy persisted beyond the injection itself. Learning linked the visual context with the event’s unfavorable value, producing avoidance when the animal could choose freely.

slides.title: Relief is rewarding specifically after injury
body: Octopuses that had received acid later preferred the lidocaine-paired chamber. Animals given saline before lidocaine did not acquire the same preference. This control separates the value of relief from a claim that lidocaine is inherently rewarding regardless of the animal’s preceding state.

**Conditioned place preference** measures increased choice of a context associated with a favorable event. The saline-plus-lidocaine control preserved the anesthetic treatment while removing prior injury. Preference developed specifically when relief followed acid exposure. The favorable value of the intervention therefore depended on the preceding state, linking local sensory suppression with learned approach to the context in which relief occurred.

slides.title: Octopus wound attention persists after the injection
body: **Discriminative pain-related behavior** is behavior directed toward the location or character of an injury. Acid-treated octopuses showed arm grooming, concealment, and skin-removal behavior localized to the injection region. Saline-treated animals did not express the same pattern.

Its persistence and suppression by local anesthesia linked injury location, ongoing sensory input and directed action. The behavioral sequence extended the evidence from learned place choice to the animal’s treatment of the affected tissue.

slides.title: The same captivity treatment affects populations differently
body: **Range-front populations** occur near the leading edge of an invasion, whereas range-core populations have been established longer. The cane-toad study applied the same general captive comparison to both groups, allowing population origin to be considered alongside the change in environment.

Range-front toads had 1,972 differentially expressed genes, compared with 951 in range-core toads. Only 504 were shared, and among shared genes the direction of change was not uniformly identical. A common captive setting therefore did not erase population-specific molecular responses.

Among genes responding in both populations, some changed in opposite directions. Captivity therefore interacted with population origin instead of producing one uniform molecular response. Comparisons of range-front and range-core biology depend on the sampling environment as well as the animals’ source populations, because both contribute to the measured expression pattern.

slides.title: Welfare inferences require converging evidence
body: The cane-toad study also measured **expression dispersion**, variation among individuals within a group. Of 155 genes with altered dispersion in range-front toads, 143 varied more among captive animals. The corresponding pattern in range-core toads was less strongly directed toward increased captive variation.

Captivity changed both average expression and individual heterogeneity. These molecular endpoints describe responses to the environment, while behavioral and intervention studies assess how animals act under altered conditions. Their combined use distinguishes a shift in biological regulation from a directly measured adverse outcome.

Mouse enrichment reduced stereotypy, rat channel enhancement changed firing and exploration, and octopus anesthesia linked sensory suppression with relief-related learning. Each intervention connected a changed condition to a particular outcome. Comparative neuroethics can evaluate which adverse processes are preventable while retaining each species’ behavioral and physiological criteria.

items.text: Complex resources reduce mouse stereotypy; full social contact predicts less macaque stereotypy. Different welfare measures can still disagree.
Repeated restraint weakens calcium-dependent afterhyperpolarization and increases lateral-amygdala firing. Enhancing the potassium-dependent brake reduces hyperexcitability.
Raphe dopamine-neuron inhibition reduces social preference after isolation; a neuronal population can also release glutamate.
Fish group and individual cortisol challenges yield different housing effects. Brain serotonin and circulating insect monoamines are different measurements.
Octopus learned avoidance, relief-dependent preference, wound attention, and ongoing afferent signals jointly support an affective injury-related state.
Cane-toad brain expression changes differ by population. Environmental history and population origin jointly shape the biological measurements used for comparison.
